title: The Sneaker Drop
mathFocus: Percentages, markup, sales tax, profit margin

scenario.setup: You're running a one-day sneaker resale booth at your school fair. You scored 5 pairs of limited-edition sneakers at wholesale price — now it's time to price them, sell them, and count your profit.
scenario.conflict: Price too high and nobody buys. Price too low and you lose money. You also need to account for sales tax so your customers pay the right amount at checkout.
scenario.objective: Price your sneakers correctly, collect the right tax, and maximize your profit

learningObjective: Apply percentage calculations for markup, sales tax, and profit margin in a real entrepreneurship scenario

questions.text: You bought 5 pairs of sneakers at the wholesale price of $45 each. What is your total wholesale cost?
questions.hint: Multiply the number of pairs by the price per pair.

questions.text: You want to apply a 40% markup to your wholesale price. What should your selling price be per pair?
questions.hint: Markup amount = $45 × 0.40. Then add that to the original price.

questions.text: Your school fair charges 8% sales tax on all purchases. A customer buys one pair at $63.00. What is the total they pay including tax?
questions.hint: Tax amount = $63.00 × 0.08. Add that to the selling price.

questions.text: You sold all 5 pairs at $63.00 each (the tax goes to the fair, not your profit). What is your profit after subtracting your wholesale cost?
What is your profit margin percentage? (Profit margin = Profit ÷ Revenue × 100)
questions.hint: Divide your profit ($90) by your total revenue ($315), then multiply by 100.
questions.explanation: Profit margin = ($90 ÷ $315) × 100 = 0.2857 × 100 ≈ 28.6%. Note: markup % and profit margin % are different numbers!

decision.prompt: You made $90 in profit from your sneaker booth. The fair happens again in 2 months. What do you do with your earnings?

options.text: Reinvest all $90 — buy 2 more pairs at wholesale ($45 each)
options.outcome: Bold reinvestment! Growing your inventory means more potential profit next time. $90 ÷ $45 = exactly 2 more pairs to sell.

options.text: Save all $90 for a bigger future launch
options.outcome: Patient and strategic! Saving your profit builds capital for a larger operation down the road — a classic business play.
Balanced approach! One new pair of inventory plus savings — you're diversifying, which reduces risk while keeping the business growing.

reflection.prompt: If you could run the sneaker booth again, would you change your 40% markup? How do you balance making a profit with keeping prices fair for your customers?

badge.name: Market Street Entrepreneur
badge.description: Ran a profitable sneaker resale booth at the school fair
